svg.text: POSITIONAL ENCODING — the MLP was never the bottleneck

a.data-tip: Feeding raw coordinates in, the network must express a rapidly varying function of a slowly varying input. Rahaman et al. showed deep networks are biased towards learning lower frequency functions, so what comes out is a smooth blur: correct at low frequency, missing every edge and texture.
a.text: Feed raw (x, y, z) and you get a blur

g.data-tip: A position normalised to the range minus 1 to 1, plus the viewing direction. Two points a hair apart look almost identical to the first layer.
Nothing is wrong with the network. It is a universal approximator; it is simply biased toward the low-frequency end.
Right in the large and wrong at every edge. Figure 4 shows geometry and texture washing out into a soft blob.

a.text: Positions are first scaled to [−1, 1]. Deep networks are biased
towards lower frequency functions, so the fit is right in the
large and wrong at every edge. Table 2 row 2: 28.77 PSNR
against 31.01, and Fig. 4 shows what that looks like.

a.data-tip: Gamma maps one scalar to a ladder of sines and cosines at frequencies that double: 2 to the 0, 2 to the 1, up to 2 to the L minus 1, each times pi times the coordinate. It has no parameters and learns nothing. Nearby coordinates that a network would otherwise struggle to separate get very different high-frequency components, so the MLP can turn a sharp corner over a tiny change in position.
a.text: Lift the coordinate first, then learn
No parameters, nothing learned: a fixed change of variables.
Two nearby points become far apart in the encoded space.

a.data-tiphead: Why L differs for position and direction
a.data-tip: Position must carry texture and sharp geometric edges, so it gets ten octaves. Viewing direction only has to describe how appearance drifts as you walk around an object, which is a smooth function of angle, so four octaves are enough. Each scalar becomes 2L numbers, applied to all three components.
a.text: Two different budgets, for a reason

g.data-tip: Ten octaves per coordinate, so each of x, y and z becomes twenty numbers: sixty in total.
Four octaves per component, so the unit direction vector becomes twenty-four numbers.

a.text: Position carries texture and hard edges. Direction only has
to describe smooth drift, so it needs far fewer octaves.

a.data-tip: Rows 7 and 8 of Table 2 sweep the number of frequencies for position. Five is too few and costs quality; fifteen buys nothing over ten. The paper attributes the ceiling to two to the L exceeding the maximum frequency present in the input images, roughly 1024 in their data. Positions are normalised to the range minus 1 to 1 before encoding, so the frequencies are relative to the scene volume; the paper gives no units for the 1024.
a.text: More frequencies stop helping, and why
Table 2, rows 7 to 9, on the realistic synthetic scenes:
Paper: the gain stops once 2 to the L passes the highest frequency
in the images, roughly 1024 = 2 to the 10: L = 10 is the ceiling.

svg.text: The idea underneath, worth stealing on its own
The network was never the bottleneck. A coordinate MLP fed raw coordinates must represent a high-frequency function of a
low-frequency input — exactly the regime it is biased against. Changing the input basis moves the problem into a regime
the same network handles easily: no extra depth, no extra width, no extra parameters.
Same trigonometric family as the Transformer positional encoding, used for an unrelated purpose. There it injects
discrete order into an order-blind architecture; here it lifts continuous coordinates so an MLP can fit sharp detail.
